It was detailed in the extreme, right down to the patterns on cut tin light sconces and various pyritized fossils appearing as decorations along some walls. The small narrow canyon began at a shallow pool at the base of a larger canyon lined in a wooden walkway that climbed toward a circular deck at the front of the home, a small low waterfall beneath it. To enclose the home, a sprawling skylight roof canopy covered the top opening of the canyon, formed of an assortment of clear, frosted, and colored disks and ovals of glass in many sizes held together like stained glass pieces. This flowed down over the gently rising canyon to the front, expanding into a rough dome shape to meet and cover the deck, like an organically fashioned 'fly's eye' dome of larger but still random sized window pieces. A free-standing portal of bent and shaped wood set into the dome held wooden door to its interior.

The main and largest room of the home, enclosed by that dome, was a roughly circular chamber filled with plants in various pots and containers and with a rampway formed along the wall leading up one storey and farther up into the slot canyon, the natural stone lined in exposed ancient marine fossils like a long fresco. Under the ramp, and along the edge of the room, a formed-in bench ran along the sandstone wall, lined with various cushions to the edge of a decorative waterfall, fed by a hole in the rock and draining to feed the small waterfall under the deck, providing a convenient way to water all those plants. Most lighting was uplighting set into the deck floor or based on luminous pots, hanging or setting on ledges. At the top of the ramp, and peak of the dome, looking out over the large main room, a circular ledge and alcove held a circular counter providing a kitchen with curious implements and fixtures. Opposite it and slightly higher on the rising rampway, a secluded chamber held a dining alcove. Carved seemingly by some persistent whirlpool that conveniently formed a perimeter seating ledge and topped with a small skylight over a hole in the top of the alcove, the dining room featured a large circular table with elaborate inlay.

The ramp continued up the narrow curving canyon, breaking into steps at intervals, the ceiling height getting lower as it went. Many more water-sculpted chambers and alcoves lined the walls, forming dark sleeping chambers lined in futons and pillows, skylit sitting rooms, shelves holding pots and various decorative stones or other artifacts, and a long flowing cabinet of carved wood. Another chamber formed a kind of bathing space formed by a waterfall from a hole in the ceiling, filling a basin-like floor, and draining into a channel and hole--presumably leading to that indoor waterfall.

As the skylight canopy reached its end, it was terminated in another bent wood portal and door which open onto a sandy forked path. To one side it opened into a sheltered rock and cactus garden, the canyon walls still forming a shallow rock wall just above head height with occasional overhangs and alcoves offering shade. The other fork turned and climbed for a bit to level off at the top of a broad mesa where a telescope on a tripod was perched. It was here that my dream lost coherence as I awoke. It was the only place I've ever felt at home.
